'''''Erythrina herbacea''''', commonly known as the '''Eastern Coralbean''',<ref name="PlantsOfLouisiana">{{Cite web |title=Erythrina herbacea |url=https://warcapps.usgs.gov/PlantID/Species/Details/3324 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250520224353/https://warcapps.usgs.gov/PlantID/Species/Details/3324 |archive-date=2025-05-20 |website=warcapps.usgs.gov}}</ref> '''Cherokee Bean''', '''Mamou''' in South Louisiana, '''Red Cardinal''', or '''Cardinal Spear''' is a [[Flowering plant|flowering]] [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] found throughout the [[southeastern United States]] and northeastern [[Mexico]];<ref name="GRIN"/> it has also been reported from parts of [[Central America]] and, as an [[introduced species]], from [[Pakistan]].  Various other systematic names have been used for this plant in the past, including ''Erythrina arborea'', ''Erythrina hederifolia'', ''Erythrina humilis'', ''Erythrina rubicunda'', ''Corallodendron herbaceum'' and ''Xyphanthus hederifolius''.

==Description==
[[File:Coralbean or Cherokee bean or Red cardinal -- Erythrina herbacea.jpg|thumb|Coral bean or Cherokee bean or Red cardinal -- Erythrina herbacea]]
Coral bean grows as a low [[shrub]] or small [[tree]], reaching around {{convert|5|m|ft|abbr=on}} in height in areas that do not kill it back by freezing;<ref name="GilNelson">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Wzmo7cHvhZkC|first=Gil |last=Nelson |title=The Trees of Florida: a Reference and Field Guide |publisher=Pineapple Press Inc. |isbn=978-1-56164-055-3 |year=1994 |page=213}}</ref> elsewhere it may only reach {{convert|1.2|m|ft|abbr=on}}.  Stems are covered in curved [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|spines]].<ref name="Duncan">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zG1v3bdd1c0C|title=Wildflowers of the Eastern United States |first=Wilbur H. |last=Duncan |author-link = Wilbur Howard Duncan |author2=Marion B. Duncan |publisher=University of Georgia Press |isbn=978-0-8203-2747-1 |year=2005 |page=39}}</ref> The [[leaf|leaves]] are yellowish-green, {{convert|15|-|20|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|6|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide.  The leaves are divided into three {{convert|2.5|-|8|cm|in|abbr=on}} [[arrowhead]]-shaped [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]].<ref name="GilNelson"/>  The bark is smooth and light gray.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.enature.com/fieldguides/detail.asp?recnum=TS0258 |title=Coral Bean ''Erythrina herbacea'' |work=FieldGuides |publisher=eNature |access-date=2009-10-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110614152229/http://www.enature.com/fieldguides/detail.asp?recnum=TS0258 |archive-date=2011-06-14 }}</ref> The tubular [[flower]]s are bright red and grow in long [[Raceme|spikes]],<ref name="NPIN">{{cite web |url=http://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=ERHE4 |title=''Erythrina herbacea'' L. |work=Native Plant Information Network |publisher=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center |access-date=2009-10-24}}</ref> each flower being {{convert|4|-|6.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} long;<ref name="GilNelson"/> the tree blooms from April to July.<ref name="Duncan"/> They are followed by {{convert|5|-|10|cm|in|abbr=on}} [[Legume|pods]] containing bright red [[seed]]s, from which the tree gets its name.<ref name="GilNelson"/> The plant forms a woody [[caudex]].<ref name="Neyland">{{cite book |first=Roy |last=Neyland |title=Wildflowers of the Coastal Plain |publisher=LSU Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-8071-3407-8 |page=131}}</ref> [[Toxin|Toxic]] [[alkaloid]]s, including [[erysopine]], [[erysothiopine]], [[erysothiovine]], [[erysovine]], [[erythrinine]], [[erythroresin]], [[coralin]], [[erythric acid]], and [[hypaphorine]],<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eS7lX_rC3GEC|title=Florida Ethnobotany |first=Daniel F. |last=Austin |publisher=CRC Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-8493-2332-4 |page=291}}</ref> are found throughout the plant. The leaves were found to contain erysotrine and erythrartine.<ref>{{cite book |last=Cordell |first=Geoffrey |title=The Alkaloids, 48|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NRESPxFMg1wC&pg=PA257 |date=26 July 1996|publisher=Academic Press |page=257 |isbn=978-0-08-086572-0}}</ref> These cause [[paralysis]] upon ingestion, much like [[curare]].<ref name="Tull">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pnnHgcasN-cC|title=Edible and Useful Plants of Texas and the Southwest: A Practical Guide |first=Delena |last=Tull |publisher=University of Texas Press |year=1999 |isbn=978-0-292-78164-1 |page=254}}</ref>

==Habitat and range==
Coral bean grows best in [[sand]]y [[soil]]s and has moderate [[Halophyte|salt tolerance]].  It is found in open woods, forest clearings, [[Hammock (ecology)|hammocks]], and [[Ruderal species|disturbed areas]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sfrc.ufl.edu/4h/Coralbean/coralbea.htm |title=Coralbean (''Erythrina herbacea'') |work=Florida Forest Plants |publisher=Florida 4-H Forest Ecology |access-date=2009-10-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100620222801/http://www.sfrc.ufl.edu/4h/Coralbean/coralbea.htm |archive-date=2010-06-20 }}</ref> In the [[United States]], it ranges from southeastern [[North Carolina]] south to [[Florida]] and west to southeastern [[Oklahoma]] and eastern [[Texas]].<ref name="Neyland"/> ''E. herbacea'' inhabits [[Tamaulipas]] in [[Mexico]].<ref name="GRIN"/>

''Erythrina herbacea'' is also found in some areas of the [[Dragoon Mountains]] in [[Southern Arizona]], located around areas of the Cochise Stronghold and other older Indian remnants. It was  most likely introduced through trade from the [[Mogollon culture]] that existed in the area from 150 AD to 1400 AD, and possibly even the later [[Apache Indians]] who occupied the area in the 19th century. Further research of the surrounding area is needed for range confirmation.{{citation needed|date=March 2014}}

==Uses==
''Erythrina herbacea'' can be readily grown in gardens within its natural range.  Although its use in gardens is not particularly common, it is popular among those who do grow it as a source of early season color, for its hardiness ([[Hardiness zone#USDA hardiness zones|USDA Zones 7-10]]), and because it attracts [[hummingbird]]s.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/birdgardenswelco01kres|url-access=registration|title=Bird Gardens: Welcoming Wild Birds to Your Yard |publisher=Brooklyn Botanic Garden |year=1998 |isbn=978-1-889538-08-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/birdgardenswelco01kres/page/56 56]}}</ref>

[[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American]] people had many [[Herbalism|medicinal]] uses for this plant, varying between nations and localities. [[Creek (people)|Creek]] women used an [[infusion]] of the root for [[bowel]] pain; the [[Choctaw]] used a [[decoction]] of the leaves as a general tonic; the [[Seminole]] used an extract of the roots for digestive problems, and extracts of the seeds, or of the inner bark, as an external rub for [[rheumatism|rheumatic]] disorders.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H8Msgmq5XbcC|title=Native American Medicinal Plants: An Ethnobotanical Dictionary |first=Daniel E. |last=Moerman |year=2009 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-88192-453-4 |page=227}}</ref>

In [[Mexico]], the seeds are used as a [[rat]] [[poison]], while a [[Fish toxins|fish poison]] is made from the bark and leaves.<ref name="Tull"/>

In some Central American countries the flowers are used in traditional cuisine. Mostly added to bean soup or meat patties, it is known for its mild narcotic properties.{{citation needed|date=March 2014}}
